passage:
For fifty years the cricket pavilion at Askerby sat at the bottom of the village field, a few yards from the river Lume: a plain timber building of 1911, with a veranda, two changing rooms and a tea room. In March 1962 a gale tore away half its roof. The committee met in April, and the secretary, Moira Callan, wrote down nearly every word.

The first thing discussed was the river. In 1947 the Lume had lain a foot deep in the changing rooms for three days, and Tobias Fenn, the groundsman, had spent the following week shovelling silt out of them with two younger members. He had distrusted the site ever since. Money was a separate worry. The club had been in debt since 1958, when a new scoreboard cost twice what Harlan Dace, the builder, had quoted, and rot was already in its posts.

Dace came with an offer. He worked mostly in brick, he said, but the timber was worth forty pounds to him if the club would sell. Then Fenn rose with a plan of his own. At the north end of the field, where the ground climbed toward a stand of beeches, the pavilion could be jacked up, set on rollers and hauled to higher ground.

The captain, Neil Pryor, argued that the gale's damage was only to the sheeting and could be repaired where it stood, but the vote went nine to four for Fenn's plan, and both of his shovelling partners were among the nine. Dace was paid to do the hauling, which took six weeks instead of two and cracked the floor in two places. Agnes Rowe, the headmistress, let the club use the village school hall for the rest of the season.

The Lume has kept to its banks every year since. The pavilion sits up among the beeches, on a floor that still tilts. Reading the minutes, it is hard to escape the sense that the committee spent its savings fleeing a river that had visited once in thirty-five years, and that the club went on paying for one frightened week long after the water had gone.

passage:
Last October the Brannock Reservoir dropped two meters in four days, so that Hester Vane, the engineer in charge of the dam, could repair its gates on the schedule she had set. The drop would leave Hollin Cove, a shallow arm with a worn gravel bar across its mouth, nearly dry; only the old river channel would stay deep. On the cove's floor lived some four thousand mussels, counted that summer by the biologist Ilse Marrow and her student Teo Arlan. A mussel can follow a falling waterline on its single foot, but slowly, about a meter a day.

The reservoir had been lowered once before, twenty years earlier, and Bram Kettle, a fisherman from Wendle, recorded it in the logbook he has kept for thirty years. The water fell just as fast that time. Beside that week's date the log reads only "cove low, gulls busy," and that line is the whole record: no one counted the mussels that autumn, living or dead.

It was Marrow who proposed the plan the team followed. At a meeting in Wendle she raised the idea of leaving the mussels where the water left them and counting how many lived. Kettle had offered to round up volunteers to carry mussels out in buckets, and Teo had sketched a wall of sandbags across the cove's mouth; a rescue, Marrow answered, would save one cove and teach nothing about the next. Odile Prask, who runs the breeding hatchery at Sallow Ford, kept two hundred mussels in her tanks for comparison.

The water fell on schedule. Teo marked out forty plots on the cove's floor and counted them every three days. About a third of the mussels in the plots followed the waterline down toward the channel; the rest stayed stranded where they were, and by November roughly half of those had died, sealed shut in the drying mud.

Marrow's figures have gone to the water authority, which will use them in planning the next drawdown. Her report runs to eleven pages, with a table for each plot.
